name: Propranolol
summary: Propranolol is a beta blocker used for heart problems such as high blood pressure and irregular heartbeats, to help with some physical symptoms of anxiety and to prevent migraines. It is available on prescription only. The NHS lists asthma, low blood pressure and a slow heart rate among reasons it may not be suitable, and describes extra effects from stopping suddenly after long-term use.
usedFor: High blood pressure and irregular heartbeats such as atrial fibrillation.
Preventing chest pain from angina and lowering the risk of future heart disease, heart attacks and strokes.
Helping with some physical symptoms of anxiety, such as a racing heart, sweating and shaking.
Easing symptoms of an overactive thyroid (thyrotoxicosis), usually alongside medicines that treat the thyroid.
Infantile haemangiomas (vascular birthmarks) in children, under specialist supervision.
howItWorks: Propranolol slows the heart rate so that the heart can pump blood around the body more easily. For anxiety, it blocks the effects of adrenaline and noradrenaline, which drive physical symptoms such as a racing heart, sweating and shaking. It therefore treats the physical symptoms of anxiety rather than the underlying worry.
onset: The NHS says it usually starts to work within a few hours, although for heart conditions or high blood pressure the full effect can take 2 to 3 weeks, and for migraine it can take several weeks to make a real difference.

common: Feeling dizzy or tired, cold hands or feet, difficulty sleeping and nightmares are the most common; the NHS says these are usually mild and short-lived.
Dizziness is most likely when starting or after a bigger dose, and the NHS says that anyone who feels dizzy should not drive, ride a bike or use tools or machinery.
Less common effects include diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting.
serious: Easy bruising, breathlessness, swollen ankles or an irregular heartbeat are rarer warning signs that need prompt medical advice from a GP or NHS 111.
Chest pain that does not settle needs a 999 call.
A serious allergic reaction, with swelling of the face or throat and difficulty breathing, is an emergency that needs a 999 call.

cautions: The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to propranolol or another medicine, low blood pressure, a slow heart rate, worsening heart failure, and lung disease or asthma among reasons it may not be suitable.
UK patient leaflets say that people who have ever had asthma or wheezing should not take propranolol tablets.
Propranolol may make it harder to recognise the warning signs of low blood sugar, so diabetes is something to mention to the doctor before starting.
Leaflets add that it can change the usual response to low blood sugar and may cause low blood sugar even in people without diabetes.
The NHS says it can be taken in pregnancy but may sometimes affect a baby's growth, so extra growth scans are usually offered from 32 weeks.
The NHS says breastfeeding is acceptable if the baby is healthy, because only tiny amounts pass into breast milk.
Some NHS headache guidance does not recommend it in pregnancy, when planning a pregnancy or during breastfeeding, so guidance differs and the clinician decides.
The NHS says other blood pressure medicines can sometimes lower blood pressure too much, causing dizziness or fainting.
Cold remedies, including pharmacy-bought ones, and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and naproxen are also listed, and the NHS says NSAIDs may raise blood pressure so are best kept to a minimum.
A hospital leaflet also lists medicines that slow the heart, such as digoxin, amiodarone, verapamil and diltiazem.
Alcohol can add to the blood-pressure-lowering effect, which can cause dizziness or light-headedness.

The NHS describes stopping suddenly after long-term use as able to cause extra effects such as an irregular heartbeat, sweating and shaking, which is why the prescriber normally lowers the dose gradually.
monitoring: The NHS says blood pressure is checked regularly for people taking it long term for migraines or anxiety.
regimenNote: Tablets, slow-release capsules and oral liquid

sections.heading: What is propranolol used for?
sections.body:
Propranolol is a beta blocker, a medicine used for heart problems, to help with some of the symptoms of anxiety and to prevent migraines. For heart conditions, the NHS lists high blood pressure, irregular heartbeats such as atrial fibrillation and preventing chest pain from angina. It is also used to lower the risk of future heart disease, heart attacks and strokes. Propranolol can ease symptoms of an overactive thyroid, where it is usually used together with medicines that treat the thyroid.

In children, specialist hospital services describe propranolol liquid being used for infantile haemangiomas, which are vascular birthmarks. Some of these specialist uses are described as off-label, meaning outside the manufacturer's licence, so guidance may differ. In the UK it is available on prescription only, as tablets, slow-release capsules or a liquid.

sections.heading: How does propranolol work, and how quickly?
sections.body:
Propranolol slows the heart rate so that the heart can pump blood more easily. For anxiety, it blocks the effects of adrenaline and noradrenaline, which drive physical symptoms such as a racing heart, sweating and shaking. This means it treats the physical symptoms of anxiety rather than the worry itself.

The NHS says it usually starts to work within a few hours. For heart conditions or high blood pressure the full effect can take 2 to 3 weeks. For migraine prevention it can take several weeks to make a real difference, so the benefit is not immediate.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of propranolol?
sections.body:
The NHS says most people have no side effects or only minor ones, and the common ones are usually mild and short-lived. The most common are feeling dizzy or tired, cold hands or feet, difficulty sleeping and nightmares. Some people get headaches, and less common effects include diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting. Dizziness is most likely when first starting or after a bigger dose, and the NHS says that anyone who feels dizzy should not drive, ride a bike or use tools or machinery.

Rarer, more serious signs include easy bruising, breathlessness, swollen ankles and an irregular heartbeat. Chest pain that does not settle needs a 999 call. A serious allergic reaction, with swelling of the face or throat and difficulty breathing, is also an emergency that needs 999. Other warning signs are usually raised with a GP or NHS 111 on the same day.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with propranolol?
sections.body:
The NHS lists several situations where propranolol may not be suitable, including a past allergic reaction to it or another medicine, low blood pressure, a slow heart rate, worsening heart failure, and lung disease or asthma. UK patient leaflets say that people who have ever had asthma or wheezing should not take propranolol tablets.

Diabetes is something to mention to the doctor before starting, because propranolol may make it harder to recognise the warning signs of low blood sugar. Leaflets add that it can change the usual response to low blood sugar and may cause low blood sugar even in people without diabetes.

On pregnancy, the NHS says propranolol can be taken but may sometimes affect a baby's growth, so extra growth scans are usually offered from 32 weeks. The NHS says breastfeeding is acceptable if the baby is healthy, because only tiny amounts pass into breast milk. Some other NHS headache guidance does not recommend it in pregnancy, when planning a pregnancy or during breastfeeding, so a clinician weighs this up for each person.

sections.heading: Taking propranolol with other medicines, alcohol and stopping
sections.body:
The NHS says that other blood pressure medicines can sometimes lower blood pressure too much, causing dizziness or fainting. Cold remedies, including pharmacy-bought ones, and NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and naproxen are also listed, and NSAIDs may raise blood pressure. A hospital leaflet lists medicines that slow the heart, such as digoxin, amiodarone, verapamil and diltiazem. Alcohol can add to the blood-pressure-lowering effect and cause dizziness or light-headedness.

The NHS describes stopping suddenly after long-term use as able to cause extra effects such as an irregular heartbeat, sweating and shaking. This is why the prescriber normally lowers the dose gradually, and why any change is decided with them.

sections.heading: Long-term use and anxiety
sections.body:
The NHS says blood pressure is checked regularly for people taking propranolol long term for migraines or anxiety. For anxiety, the NHS says there do not seem to be lasting harmful effects from taking it for several months or years, and that it is best taken only for as long as needed. Many doctors prefer treatments that do not involve medicine for anxiety, including talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy.

A local NHS medicines alert says NICE does not recommend propranolol for generalised anxiety disorder or panic disorder in adults, and warns that it is toxic in overdose. Anyone in immediate danger can call 999, use NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or call Samaritans free on 116 123 at any time.

faqs.a: The NHS says propranolol can help with some of the symptoms of anxiety. It works on physical symptoms such as a racing heart, sweating and shaking, and is usually taken for a short time. Local NHS guidance is more cautious, so whether it suits a person is for their clinician to decide.

The NHS says propranolol will not stop contraception working. However, the combined pill and contraceptive patch are not usually recommended with propranolol or other blood pressure medicines. Vomiting or prolonged diarrhoea can also make the pill less effective.

faqs.q: Can people with diabetes have propranolol?
faqs.a: Diabetes is something the NHS says to tell the doctor about before starting propranolol. The medicine may make it harder to recognise the warning signs of low blood sugar. Anyone who has low blood sugar without the usual warning signs is advised by the NHS to speak to their doctor.

faqs.q: Can people drive while taking propranolol?
faqs.a: Propranolol can make some people feel dizzy, especially when first starting or after a bigger dose. The NHS says anyone affected should not drive, ride a bike or use tools or machinery. It also says the decision about whether it is safe to drive rests with the individual, and if in doubt they should not drive.

faqs.q: What happens if propranolol is stopped suddenly?
faqs.a: The NHS describes extra effects after stopping suddenly following long-term use, such as an irregular heartbeat, sweating and shaking. For this reason the prescriber normally lowers the dose gradually, and decides how.

faqs.q: Is Inderal the same as propranolol?
faqs.a: Inderal is a UK brand name of propranolol hydrochloride tablets, made by Atnahs Pharma UK. Other UK products include modified-release capsules and an oral solution.
